s.f: \int\sin x=-\cos x,\ \int\cos x=\sin x,\ \int\sec^2x=\tan x,\ \int\csc^2x=-\cot x,\ \int\sec x\tan x=\sec x,\ \int\csc x\cot x=-\csc x

s.q: Integrals of tan, cot, sec, csc
s.f: \int\tan x\,dx=\ln|\sec x|,\quad\int\cot x\,dx=\ln|\sin x|,\quad\int\sec x\,dx=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|,\quad\int\csc x\,dx=\ln\left|\tan\tfrac x2\right|
s.d: $\int\sec x\,dx=\int\frac{\sec x(\sec x+\tan x)}{\sec x+\tan x}dx$; numerator is the derivative of the denominator.
By parts with $u=\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, $dv=dx$, then add the integral back to both sides.

s.q: Integrals of hyperbolic and exponential forms

s.h: ILATE: Inverse, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — choose $u$ from the left.

s.q: By parts with a cyclic integral
s.f: I=\int e^x\sin x\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ 2I=e^x(\sin x-\cos x)\ \Rightarrow\ I=\frac{e^x}2(\sin x-\cos x)
\int x^ne^{ax}dx:\ \text{alternate signs of } u,u',u'',\ldots\ \text{times successive integrals of } e^{ax}
\int\sin^mx\cos^nx\,dx:\ m\ \text{odd}\to t=\cos x;\ n\ \text{odd}\to t=\sin x;\ m+n\ \text{negative even}\to t=\tan x
p\in\mathbb Z:\ \text{expand};\ \tfrac{m+1}n\in\mathbb Z:\ t^k=a+bx^n;\ \tfrac{m+1}n+p\in\mathbb Z:\ t^k=ax^{-n}+b
\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{\tan x-1}{\sqrt{2\tan x}}+\frac1{2\sqrt2}\ln\left|\frac{\tan x-\sqrt{2\tan x}+1}{\tan x+\sqrt{2\tan x}+1}\right|+C

s.n: Add or subtract and halve for the individual integrals.

s: If this type comes, solve like this

s.q: If the numerator is a combination of the denominator and its derivative ($\int\frac{ae^x+be^{-x}}{ce^x+de^{-x}}$, $\frac{a\sin x+b\cos x}{c\sin x+d\cos x}$)
s.s: Write the numerator as $A(\text{denominator})+B(\text{derivative of denominator})$. || Compare coefficients of $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$ (or $\sin$, $\cos$) to get $A$, $B$. || The integral is $Ax+B\ln|\text{Den}|+C$. || Match with the given form.

s.q: If the integrand has $\frac{x^2\pm1}{x^4+kx^2+1}$ or $\tan^{-1}\frac{x^2+1}x$ (divide by $x^2$)
s.s: Split the integrand into simpler fractions. || Divide numerator and denominator by $x^2$. || For $x^2-1$ put $t=x+\frac1x$; for $x^2+1$ put $t=x-\frac1x$. || Note $\frac d{dx}\tan^{-1}(x+\frac1x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x^4+3x^2+1}$, so the first piece is $\int\frac{dT}T=\ln T$. || Write $1=\frac12[(x^2+1)-(x^2-1)]$ to split a plain $\frac1{x^4+kx^2+1}$.
s.e: First piece: $\ln\left(\tan^{-1}\frac{x^2+1}x\right)$; the remaining $\int\frac{dx}{x^4+3x^2+1}$ splits into $\frac1{2\sqrt5}\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1/x}{\sqrt5}-\frac12\tan^{-1}(x+\frac1x)$.

s.q: If $\sin$ and $\cos$ appear with powers whose sum is a negative even integer (or $\sin^3+\cos^3$ in the denominator)
s.s: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^{|m+n|}x$ so everything is in $\tan x$ and $\sec^2x$. || Put $t=\tan x$, $dt=\sec^2xdx$; use $\sec^2x=1+t^2$ for leftover powers. || Integrate the resulting rational/power function (partial fractions for $\frac t{t^3+1}$). || Return to $\tan x$ (or $\cot x$).

s.q: If the integrand is $\frac{\cos x}{\sin^3x(1+\sin^6x)^{2/3}}$ type (take out the highest power)
s.r: A power of $(1+t^n)$ times a power of $t$, after $t=\sin x$.
s.s: Put $t=\sin x$. || Take the highest power of $t$ out of the bracket. || Substitute $u=1+t^{-n}$; $du=-nt^{-n-1}dt$. || Integrate the power of $u$ and return.
Divide inside to write the integrand as $\frac1{(x-b)^2}\left(\frac{x-a}{x-b}\right)^{-p}$. || Put $t=\frac{x-a}{x-b}$. || Integrate the power of $t$.

s.q: If two different roots of $x$ appear ($x^{2/3}$ and $x^{1/2}$)
s.s: Put $x=t^L$ with $L$ the lcm of the root orders. || All powers become integers; simplify. || Divide polynomials and integrate. || Use the given value to fix $C$.

s.q: If the integrand is $e^x[f+f']$ or $[xf'+f]$ in disguise
s.r: "$\int\left(\frac x{x\sin x+\cos x}\right)^2dx$", "$\int\frac{1-\sin(\ln t)}{1-\cos(\ln t)}dt$", "$\int\left((\frac xe)^{2x}+(\frac ex)^{2x}\right)\ln x\,dx$".
s.s: Look for a substitution that produces $e^u$ (e.g. $t=e^u$ when $\ln t$ appears). || Split the remaining factor into $f+f'$: for half angles, $\frac{1-\sin u}{1-\cos u}=\frac12\csc^2\frac u2-\cot\frac u2$. || Read off $e^uf(u)$. || For $(\frac xe)^{2x}$, differentiate it directly — it already gives $\ln x$.

s.q: If it is $\int x^n\sin x$ or $\int x^ne^x$ (repeated parts)
s.f: \int x^3\sin x=-x^3\cos x+3x^2\sin x+6x\cos x-6\sin x;\quad g'=\text{integrand}
s.s: Use the tabular (DI) method: differentiate $x^n$ down to 0, integrate $\sin x$ repeatedly, alternate signs. || Note $g'(x)$ is just the integrand. || Substitute the point.

For $(ax^2+b)\sqrt{cx^2+d}$: put $x=\frac1t$, then $u^2=dt^2+c$ — it reduces to $\int\frac{du}{\text{quadratic}}$. || For $\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}$: rationalise to $\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, split into $\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}-\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. || Use the given value to fix the constant.

s.f: \int\frac{P(x)}{\sqrt Q}dx=(\text{poly of degree one less})\sqrt Q+\lambda\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt Q}
s.s: Assume the answer form with unknown coefficients. || Differentiate both sides and multiply by $\sqrt Q$. || Compare coefficients to find them.
Complete the square: $(x+\frac12)^2+\frac34$. || Use the reduction formula (or $x+\frac12=\frac{\sqrt3}2\tan\theta$). || Compare with the given form.

s.q: If the integrand has powers of $\sqrt{1+x^2}+x$
s.s: Put $t=\sqrt{1+x^2}+x$; then $\sqrt{1+x^2}-x=\frac1t$, so the integrand is $t^{19}$. || $x=\frac12(t-\frac1t)$ gives $dx$. || Integrate the powers of $t$ and rewrite.

s.q: If the integrand is the derivative of a quotient (high powers over a squared polynomial)
s.s: Divide numerator and denominator by the power that makes the denominator $(\ldots+\text{const})^2$ (here $x^{18}$). || The numerator becomes minus the derivative of the new bracket. || Answer $\frac1u$, then simplify back.
